title: GMAT Focus Data Insights Practice Test 30
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt:
Goods in and goods out at five depots, in tonnes:

Ashby: 4,200 in, 3,780 out
Bardon: 2,900 in, 3,190 out
Colwich: 3,300 in, 3,234 out
Dunham: 1,500 in, 1,950 out
Elston: 6,400 in, 6,080 out

Which depot comes closest to shipping out as much as it takes in?
questions.explanation: Goods in divided by goods out: Ashby 1.111, Bardon 0.909, Colwich 1.020, Dunham 0.769, Elston 1.053. A perfectly balanced depot would score 1.000, and Colwich is nearest at 1.020. Elston handles by far the most tonnage but runs a wider gap between the two figures, and two depots ship out more than they take in.

questions.prompt:
Annual figures:

2018: 410
2019: 385
2020: 452
2021: 498
2022: 461
2023: 470
2024: 445

Which two consecutive years have the largest combined total?
questions.explanation: Adding each adjacent pair: 2018 and 2019 795, 2019 and 2020 837, 2020 and 2021 950, 2021 and 2022 959, 2022 and 2023 931, 2023 and 2024 915. 2021 and 2022 is largest at 959. The single highest year is 2021, and it appears in two of these pairs — but the pair that wins is the one where the year beside it is strongest, not the one containing the peak alone.

questions.prompt:
Five bids, each quoted in its own currency. One pound buys 1.16 euros or 1.27 dollars:

Bid A: 41,200 GBP
Bid B: 46,400 EUR
Bid C: 49,530 USD
Bid D: 44,080 EUR
Bid E: 38,500 GBP

Which bid is cheapest once every figure is put into sterling?
questions.explanation: Converting each to pounds: Bid A GBP 41,200.00, Bid B GBP 40,000.00, Bid C GBP 39,000.00, Bid D GBP 38,000.00, Bid E GBP 38,500.00. Bid D is cheapest at GBP 38,000.00. The largest number in the table belongs to Bid C, which is not the dearest bid at all once its dollars are converted.

questions.prompt:
Seven readings, in order: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30

The largest reading is then corrected from 30 to 72. Which statement about the effect is accurate?
options: A. Both the mean and the median rise
E. The mean rises by 6 and the range more than triples, but the median does not move
questions.explanation: Before: mean 21, median 21, range 18. After: mean 27, median 21, range 60. Changing the largest value moves the total, and so the mean, and stretches the range from 18 to 60. The median is the fourth of seven readings whichever way the seventh moves, so it stays exactly where it was.

questions.prompt:
A rectangle has a perimeter of 84 cm, and its length and width are in the ratio 4 : 3.

Select the length AND the width.
options: E. The two sides cannot be worked out from a ratio
questions.explanation: The perimeter counts each side twice, so one length plus one width is 42 cm. Split in the ratio 4 : 3, that is 7 parts of 6 cm: 24 cm and 18 cm. Splitting the whole 84 cm instead of half of it gives 48 cm and 36 cm, which would need a perimeter of 168 cm.

questions.prompt:
A jacket cost GBP 127.50 after a 15% discount.

Select the price before the discount AND the amount saved.
questions.explanation: GBP 127.50 is 85% of the original price, so the original is GBP 127.50 / 0.85 = GBP 150.00 and the saving GBP 22.50. Adding 15% back to GBP 127.50 gives GBP 146.63, because 15% of the reduced price is less than 15% of the full one.

questions.prompt:
Two retail chains:

Chain One: 45 shops, averaging GBP 68,000.00 of turnover each
Chain Two: 12 shops, averaging GBP 310,000.00 of turnover each

Select the chain with more shops AND the chain with the larger total turnover.
options: A. Chain One on both measures
B. Chain Two on both measures
C. Chain Two on shops; Chain One on turnover
D. Chain One on shops; Chain Two on turnover
E. The two chains are equal on both measures
questions.explanation: Shop counts are given: Chain One 45, Chain Two 12. Total turnover is shops multiplied by the average: Chain One GBP 3,060,000.00 and Chain Two GBP 3,720,000.00. The larger chain has almost four times as many shops, but each takes barely a fifth as much, so the smaller chain turns over more.

questions.prompt:
A taxi charges GBP 14.60 for a 8 km journey and GBP 24.20 for a 14 km journey, on the same tariff.

Select the charge per kilometre AND the fixed charge that applies whatever the distance.
options: A. GBP 1.83 a km; GBP 1.80 fixed
B. GBP 1.60 a km; GBP 1.80 fixed
C. GBP 1.60 a km; GBP 2.40 fixed
D. GBP 1.73 a km; nothing fixed
E. The tariff cannot be worked out from two journeys
questions.explanation: The extra 6 km cost GBP 9.60, so each kilometre is GBP 1.60. The 8 km journey therefore has GBP 12.80 of distance charge in it, leaving GBP 1.80 that does not depend on distance. Dividing a single fare by its distance gives GBP 1.83 a km and buries the fixed charge inside the rate.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (table): patients registered — Practice P 9,600, Practice Q 4,200, Practice R 15,400

SOURCE 2 (table): doctors in post — Practice P 6, Practice Q 3, Practice R 11

SOURCE 3 (memo): "The additional doctor goes to the practice carrying the most patients for each doctor already in post."

Which practice receives the additional doctor?
options: C. The three practices are equal
D. Cannot be determined from the sources
questions.explanation: Patients divided by doctors: Practice P 1,600, Practice Q 1,400, Practice R 1,400. Practice P carries the heaviest list per doctor. Practice R has 15,400 patients, more than the other two together, but 11 doctors to share them.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (report): "Delays fell from 18% of services to 6%."

SOURCE 2 (note): from January a train counts as delayed only if it is more than 15 minutes late. The old threshold was 5 minutes.

SOURCE 3 (table): trains arriving between 5 and 15 minutes late made up 11% of services in both years.

Which statement is best supported?
options: A. Trains are three times as punctual as they were
B. Almost the whole fall comes from the change of threshold: on the new definition the old year would have shown 7%, against 6% now
C. Delays actually rose once the two years are measured the same way
D. The change of threshold made no difference to the figure
E. 11% of trains are late every year whatever the threshold
questions.explanation: Of the 18% late by the old five-minute rule, 11 points were between 5 and 15 minutes late, so only 7% were more than 15 minutes late — the measure now in use. Against that 7%, this year's 6% is an improvement of 1 point, not 12. The service got slightly better; the headline got much better.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (table): rate a kilometre — Haulier A GBP 4.20, Haulier B GBP 5.40, Haulier C GBP 4.85

SOURCE 2 (table): hazardous-goods licence — Haulier A none; Hauliers B and C both licensed.

SOURCE 3 (email): "The load is classed as hazardous. Use the cheapest haulier licensed to carry it."

Which haulier should be used?
options: D. All three cost the same
E. Cannot be determined from the sources
questions.explanation: Haulier A is cheapest at GBP 4.20 a kilometre but holds no hazardous-goods licence, so it cannot carry this load at any price. Of the two that are licensed, Haulier B at GBP 5.40 and Haulier C at GBP 4.85, Haulier C is cheaper by GBP 0.55 a kilometre.

questions.prompt:
SOURCE 1 (table): sales rose 9% over the year while the number of customers fell 4%.

SOURCE 2 (note): the product range was unchanged throughout.

SOURCE 3 (memo): no price was changed at any point in the year.

Which explanation of the rise in sales do the sources rule out?
options: A. Each remaining customer bought more than before
B. The average order grew over the year
C. The rise cannot be put down to higher prices
D. The rise came from attracting more customers
E. Fewer customers spent more between them
questions.explanation: Source 1 says the customer count fell, so more customers cannot be the explanation — that is the one option the sources close off. Source 3 rules out price as well, which leaves each remaining customer buying more; the other four options are all ways of saying that, or of stating what has been ruled out.

questions.prompt:
What is the length of a rectangle?

(1) Its area is 96 square centimetres.
(2) Its width is 8 centimetres.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) fits 12 by 8, 24 by 4 and 96 by 1, all with different lengths. (2) gives a width with no area to divide it into. Together, 96 divided by 8 gives a length of 12 cm. Each statement supplies exactly one of the two things needed.

questions.prompt:
Is the average of four numbers a whole number?

(1) All four numbers are whole numbers.
(2) Their sum is greater than 20.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: Four whole numbers summing to 28 average 7, a whole number; four summing to 26 average 6.5, which is not. Both cases satisfy the two statements together, so even combined they leave the answer open. What matters is whether the sum divides by four, and neither statement says.

questions.prompt:
How far did a car travel?

(1) It used 32 litres of fuel.
(2) It drove for 3 hours at a steady 76 km/h.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) gives fuel with no consumption rate attached, so the distance could be anything. (2) is distance in disguise: 3 hours at 76 km/h is 228 km. Only the second statement bears on the question, and it settles it outright.

questions.prompt:
Is the positive integer n a multiple of 15?

(1) n is a multiple of 30.
(2) n is a multiple of 5.
options: A. Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
B. Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
C. BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER alone is sufficient.
D. EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
E. Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: Every multiple of 30 is a multiple of 15, since 30 is twice 15, so (1) answers the question with a definite yes. (2) admits 10 and 20, which are not multiples of 15, as well as 15 and 30, which are. The two are consistent, since 30 is also a multiple of 5.

questions.prompt:
Which clinic runs the most appointments through each of its rooms?

Clinic | Appointments (thousands) | Rooms | Staff | Missed appointments
Ashgrove | 42 | 8 | 45 | 6.4%
Bellwood | 18 | 4 | 29 | 9.1%
Cranfell | 76 | 14 | 92 | 4.2%
Dovecote | 31 | 7 | 55 | 7.6%
Everton | 58 | 9 | 77 | 5.1%
Fernhill | 12 | 3 | 21 | 11.3%
questions.explanation: Appointments divided by rooms: Ashgrove 5.25 thousand, Bellwood 4.5 thousand, Cranfell 5.43 thousand, Dovecote 4.43 thousand, Everton 6.44 thousand, Fernhill 4 thousand. Everton works its rooms hardest at 6.44 thousand each. Cranfell runs 76 thousand appointments, more than any other, but has 14 rooms to run them through.

questions.prompt:
Which clinic loses the most appointments a year to non-attendance?

Clinic | Appointments (thousands) | Rooms | Staff | Missed appointments
Ashgrove | 42 | 8 | 45 | 6.4%
Bellwood | 18 | 4 | 29 | 9.1%
Cranfell | 76 | 14 | 92 | 4.2%
Dovecote | 31 | 7 | 55 | 7.6%
Everton | 58 | 9 | 77 | 5.1%
Fernhill | 12 | 3 | 21 | 11.3%
questions.explanation: Missed appointments are the total multiplied by the rate: Ashgrove 2,688, Bellwood 1,638, Cranfell 3,192, Dovecote 2,356, Everton 2,958, Fernhill 1,356. Cranfell loses the most — and it has the best attendance record in the table at 4.2%. Fernhill misses 11.3% of its appointments, nearly three times the rate, but runs so few that it loses 1,356 of them.

questions.prompt:
How many clinics have a missed-appointment rate above the median and fewer than 50 staff?

Clinic | Appointments (thousands) | Rooms | Staff | Missed appointments
Ashgrove | 42 | 8 | 45 | 6.4%
Bellwood | 18 | 4 | 29 | 9.1%
Cranfell | 76 | 14 | 92 | 4.2%
Dovecote | 31 | 7 | 55 | 7.6%
Everton | 58 | 9 | 77 | 5.1%
Fernhill | 12 | 3 | 21 | 11.3%
questions.explanation: The median missed-appointment rate is 7%. Above it: Bellwood 9.1%, Dovecote 7.6%, Fernhill 11.3%. Fewer than 50 staff: Ashgrove 45, Bellwood 29, Fernhill 21. On both counts: Bellwood and Fernhill — 2. One small clinic keeps its missed rate below the median, so size does not settle it on its own.

questions.prompt:
Which clinic handles the most appointments for each member of staff?

Clinic | Appointments (thousands) | Rooms | Staff | Missed appointments
Ashgrove | 42 | 8 | 45 | 6.4%
Bellwood | 18 | 4 | 29 | 9.1%
Cranfell | 76 | 14 | 92 | 4.2%
Dovecote | 31 | 7 | 55 | 7.6%
Everton | 58 | 9 | 77 | 5.1%
Fernhill | 12 | 3 | 21 | 11.3%
questions.explanation: Appointments divided by staff: Ashgrove 933, Bellwood 621, Cranfell 826, Dovecote 564, Everton 753, Fernhill 571. Ashgrove leads at 933 a head. That makes three different clinics across these table questions: Everton runs the most through each room, Cranfell loses the most appointments to non-attendance, and Ashgrove gets the most out of each member of staff.
